title: Forecasters Warn of a Potentially Historic El Niño—Here's Why It Matters
summary: An El Niño brewing in the Pacific is shaping up to be a heavyweight. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) announced Thursday that this year's event has an 81% chance of reaching the top-tier "very strong" category by fall. If it does, it would rank among the most intense since tracking began in 1950. "This is not a run-of-the-mill El Niño," said climate scientist Daniel Swain. It's already zipped past the weak stage and is now moderate, with no signs of slowing. Ocean temperatures in key monitoring regions are at or near record highs for this time of year, partly because the natural cycle is amplifying the background warming from human-caused climate change. "It's pretty extreme," said Emily Becker of the University of Miami. "Not unprecedented, but very unusual." The impacts could be far-reaching. El Niño typically brings a rainier winter to the southern U.S., a warmer winter to the northern U.S. and Canada, and suppresses Atlantic hurricane activity—Colorado State University just slashed its storm forecast. Globally, it can trigger droughts in Indonesia and deluges in the eastern Pacific. The 1997-1998 super El Niño led to 23,000 deaths and $45 billion in damages. But Swain cautions that because this one is unfolding on a hotter planet, "we might not expect to see the exact same impacts." El Niño acts as a planetary thermostat, releasing stored ocean heat into the atmosphere. Many scientists now predict that 2027 will surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record. "A strong El Niño would raise the odds of dramatic new climate records over the next 6 to 12 months," said Zack Labe of Climate Central. It's a stark reminder that natural variability and human-driven warming are increasingly intertwined.
why_it_matters: This El Niño could disrupt farming, water supplies, and economies across the globe just as the world is already struggling with extreme weather. It's a powerful example of how natural cycles and human-caused climate change team up to shape the future environment you'll inherit.

background_read: El Niño is a natural climate pattern that occurs every two to seven years when the trade winds weaken and warm water piles up in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. The last very strong event, in 2015-2016, pushed global temperatures to then-record highs and caused severe droughts, floods, and coral bleaching.

The 1997-1998 super El Niño remains one of the most destructive, with devastating impacts from mudslides in California to famine in Papua New Guinea. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) tracks these events using a network of ocean buoys and satellites.

Climate scientist Daniel Swain of UCLA and Emily Becker of the University of Miami are among the experts warning that this El Niño is being amplified by human-driven warming, making its effects harder to predict. Zack Labe of Climate Central points out that the extra heat could push the planet past dangerous temperature milestones.

perspectives.description: For drought-stricken parts of the southern United States, the extra rain could ease water shortages. A suppressed Atlantic hurricane season also lowers the risk of catastrophic storms for coastal communities, which could save lives and reduce damage.

A very strong El Niño can trigger deadly floods in Peru and Ecuador, crippling droughts in Southeast Asia and Australia, and wildfires in the Amazon. On top of that, the release of ocean heat is likely to shatter global temperature records, worsening heat waves and ice melt.

El Niño has existed for millennia, but its behavior is now being altered by greenhouse gases. Scientists see this event as a test case: how do natural oscillations behave when the planet's background temperature is higher? The answer will sharpen climate models and warning systems.

Preparing for El Niño's effects—like flood defenses in California or drought plans in India—can reduce suffering. This event also adds urgency to cutting emissions, because if even natural cycles become turbo-charged, the world faces more frequent and intense disasters.
